clue.text: Sick of France after drinking European tea, say

indicators.note: to drink something is to take it inside, so the French word swallows the letter for 'European'

blocks.note: French for bad or ill, as in mal de mer
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone feeling queasy in France after a cup of European tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea' here is not the drink but the evening meal, as many Britons call dinner; 'say' flags it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage tea is also an early evening main repast, so it is one example of the wider category.

clue.text: Sort of ball made square after manipulation

indicators.note: manipulated things are handled and rearranged, so the two words 'made square' get reordered

blocks.note: the ten letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A ball being squashed into a cube shape by someone's hands.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a physical ball, but it is a dance: a MASQUERADE is a ball where guests wear masks.
explanation.definitionFit: A masked dance event is one particular kind of formal party, hence a sort of ball.

clue.text: Go off about backsliding in-house worker?

indicators.note: sliding back in a down entry means the joined pieces run upward, read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: food that goes off will rot
circa, used for approximate dates

explanation.surface: A domestic servant slipping back into bad habits and going off in a huff.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a pun: 'in-house' means working in a playhouse, a theatre, not in a home.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer does their job inside a theatre, which crosswords often call a house.

clue.text: Teach gloomy poet to grasp piece from Eliot

indicators.note: the poet grasps, holding the selected letter inside his arms
a single piece taken from the name, here its opening letter

blocks.note: as in a black mood
a traditional word for a poet
the first letter of the poet's name

explanation.surface: A glum poet teaching a class, holding up an extract from T. S. Eliot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teach' is a capitalised surname, not a verb: Edward Teach was the pirate known as Blackbeard. The capital at the start of the clue hides this.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Teach was the real surname of the notorious early eighteenth-century pirate captain.

clue.text: Room height forcing head down a touch

indicators.note: the first letter of the height word is pushed one place further down the entry, rearranging it

blocks.note: height above sea level

explanation.surface: A low-ceilinged room where you must duck your head slightly.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the leading A moves, one place down, so ALTITUDE becomes LATITUDE; 'Room' means scope, not a chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: Room in the sense of freedom or scope to act is a standard synonym for leeway.

clue.text: Key stuck in public lav I salvaged

indicators.note: the answer is stuck inside the run of words that follows, across their boundaries

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of 'public' into 'salvaged'

explanation.surface: A key jammed in the lock of a public toilet, which someone has rescued.
explanation.walkthrough: CLAVIS is Latin for key, occasionally used in English for a glossary or key to a text.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin noun for a key, also used in English for an explanatory guide to a cipher or text.

clue.text: Where Jack might end up sounds unacceptable

indicators.note: we are told the phrase describing Jack only needs to sound right, not be spelt right

blocks.note: in the nursery rhyme Jack falls down the hill after fetching a pail of water, so he lands past it

explanation.surface: Speculating on where some fellow called Jack will finish, which seems shocking.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water; Jack fell down' supplies the picture of Jack tumbling past the bucket.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes conduct outside the bounds of decency, originally a fenced boundary.

clue.text: No enjoyable existence if gas and dole cut

indicators.note: cut up means chopped into bits, so the letters of the three fodder words are jumbled

blocks.note: 'and' just joins, the fodder is 'if', 'gas' and 'dole'

explanation.surface: Life would be miserable if heating and benefit payments were both slashed.
explanation.walkthrough: The dole is British slang for unemployment benefit; 'and' joins the fodder words and is not part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom denotes a wretched, miserable way of living, the opposite of a pleasant time.

clue.text: They won’t go off clothes of a retro style

blocks.note: shells or fireworks that fail to explode
an old-fashioned slang word for garments

explanation.surface: Vintage garments that never go out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go off' reads as going stale or out of style, but here it means exploding.
explanation.definitionFit: Failed munitions are called by this word, and it is also dated slang for one's garments.

clue.text: Fabric modelled on openwork fabric one models

blocks.note: an artist's model sat for the painter
the roman numeral
a mesh fabric with open holes, the setter reusing 'fabric'
surface padding echoing 'modelled'; it supplies no letters

explanation.surface: A fashion house describing a cloth whose design copies lace.
explanation.walkthrough: SATINET is a thin or imitation satin. The final 'models' does no work in the wordplay and is best read as surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a woven cloth, a thin imitation of satin, so it is a kind of textile.

clue.text: Ordinary reason drinks-lover avoids McDonalds?

blocks.note: the everyday idiom for mediocre
read literally: the milkshakes there are not very good

explanation.surface: An everyday explanation for why someone who loves drinks skips a fast-food chain.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half takes the idiom literally: McDonald's sells milkshakes, and a connoisseur might judge them poor.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means unremarkable or mediocre, nothing special at all.

clue.text: Whatever happens in North Broadway?

blocks.note: Northern English dialect for 'anyway' or 'in any case'
a broad way, read as a route of any kind

explanation.surface: A question about whether anything at all goes on in a street called North Broadway.
explanation.walkthrough: ANYROAD is heard in Yorkshire and Lancashire meaning 'anyway'; the question mark allows the whimsical reading of Broadway as a broad way, i.e. any road.
explanation.definitionFit: In northern dialect the word is used for 'in any case', regardless of what occurs.

clue.text: Music producers unfortunately pain this group

indicators.note: things that go unfortunately go wrong, so the following words come out in a bad order

blocks.note: all thirteen letters of the three words

explanation.surface: Record producers are an unfortunate source of annoyance for a band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Music producers' suggests people in a studio; here it means instruments that produce music.
explanation.definitionFit: Vertical-strung keyboard instruments generate sound, so they literally produce tunes.

clue.text: Unqualified pharmacists up on latest trends in business

blocks.note: people supplying drugs without a licence
fashionable, up to date

explanation.surface: Chemists without proper qualifications keeping up with commercial fads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pharmacists' suggests chemists, but unqualified ones are drug pushers; in a down entry 'up on' stacks the first part above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A franchise selling a maker's products, like a car showroom, is a commercial enterprise.

clue.text: Corbynistas to tax loaf and ginger nuts

indicators.note: to tax is to burden, so the left-wingers carry the loaf inside themselves

blocks.note: supporters of left-wing Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, so socialists
as in 'use your loaf', from rhyming slang loaf of bread for head

explanation.surface: Corbyn supporters proposing a levy on bread and ginger biscuits.
explanation.walkthrough: Ginger nuts are British biscuits, but here nut means head, so ginger nuts are ginger-haired heads.
explanation.definitionFit: Nut is slang for a person's skull, so ginger-coloured ones belong to people with auburn hair.

clue.text: Gin diet so fantastic it helps with a breakdown

indicators.note: something fantastic is wildly unreal, so the letters are freely rearranged

blocks.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A diet of gin sounds great for coping with a nervous collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breakdown' suggests a mental collapse, but it is the breaking down of food in the gut.
explanation.definitionFit: The bodily process turns eaten food into simpler substances, dismantling meals into nutrients.

clue.text: Holiday to Egypt is a load of rubbish

blocks.note: a short journey away
international vehicle registration code

explanation.surface: A complaint that a trip to Egypt turned out to be dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: E is Egypt's international car registration letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe is stomach lining, and figuratively means nonsense or worthless talk.

clue.text: One could blow up dinghy or commit hit in Bow, Spooner said

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of pairs of words

blocks.note: to commit something to paper is to put it there
Bow is in the East End, where Cockneys say th as f

explanation.surface: Someone could sabotage a small boat, or carry out a gangland hit in East London.
explanation.walkthrough: Say PUT FUMP and swap the first sounds to get 'fut pump'. Bow is a Cockney district of east London.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflatable boat is filled with air by a pedal-operated device, so it can inflate one.

clue.text: Really like the Thing’s finger

blocks.note: slang for enjoy or appreciate, from 1930s jazz talk
the pronoun that stands for any thing

explanation.surface: Admiration for a finger belonging to Thing, the disembodied hand of the Addams Family.
explanation.walkthrough: Thing in the Addams Family is just a hand, which makes the finger apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Digit is the anatomical and formal word for a finger or toe.

clue.text: Predict warning given to guy who targeted Apple

blocks.note: the golfer's shout to people in the ball's path
William Tell shot an apple off his son's head

explanation.surface: Forecasting a warning sent to a hacker who went after the tech giant.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital A makes Apple look like the company, but it is the fruit William Tell shot with his crossbow.
explanation.definitionFit: To foretell is to declare in advance what will happen, a plain synonym for forecasting.

clue.text: Flash risible leader? One’s into that!

definitions.text: Flash risible leader? One’s into that!

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here of 'risible'
the numeral word goes into the combination of the others

blocks.note: a moment, as in 'in a flash' or 'just a mo'
taken as written
its leading letter

explanation.surface: A cheeky prankster who likes flashing, the ridiculous ringleader.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes someone who bares their bottom as a laughable prank and is keen on it; 'Flash' is not exposure but a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: Mooning means baring one's buttocks as a joke, so a practitioner is a risible flasher.

clue.text: One whose pupils are not yet fully developed?

definitions.text: One whose pupils are not yet fully developed?

blocks.clueFragment: pupils are not yet fully developed
blocks.note: surface: the eyes of someone whose pupils have an abnormality
setter's reading: the pupils are children being taught, who are still growing

explanation.surface: An eye doctor's observation about a patient with immature pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupils' reads as parts of the eye, but it means students in a class.
explanation.definitionFit: An educator in a primary or secondary setting has young learners who have not grown up.

clue.text: Stockings wrapped round face of Rodney Trotter?

indicators.note: the stockings are wrapped round the letter taken from the name
the face of a word is its front, its first letter

blocks.note: hosiery
its opening letter

explanation.surface: Rodney Trotter, the hapless younger brother in the British sitcom Only Fools and Horses, with stockings over his head.
explanation.walkthrough: Rodney Trotter is a character from the British sitcom Only Fools and Horses; 'Trotter' is split off as the definition, a creature that trots.
explanation.definitionFit: The question mark flags a definition by example: a trotting animal, such as a harness racer.

clue.text: Chartered accountant involved in S&M racket

indicators.note: the accountant is involved in, so placed inside, the letters of the kinky abbreviation

blocks.note: sadomasochism, taken letter for letter
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A professional bookkeeper caught up in a seedy fetish business.
explanation.walkthrough: The ampersand is ignored; S and M hold CA between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a fraudulent money-making scheme, so a swindle or con.

clue.text: Yellow that comes from egg

blocks.note: cowardly
a hatchling bird

explanation.surface: Yolk colour, the part that comes out of an egg.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at the yolk; yellow means cowardly instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a slang word for cowardly and the farmyard bird that hatches from a shell.

clue.text: Discover a foreign article on the place you live

blocks.note: the French word for a
our planet

explanation.surface: Finding an overseas newspaper piece about your home town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper piece, but it is the grammatical word 'a', here in French.
explanation.definitionFit: To dig up or bring to light something hidden is to find it.

clue.text: MS unit ramps up screening considerably at first

indicators.note: things that are up are in disorder, so the two words get rearranged
to screen is to shield, holding the extra letter within
only the opening letter of the preceding word is taken

blocks.note: the nine letters to rearrange
its first letter

explanation.surface: A multiple sclerosis unit greatly increasing its screening programme.
explanation.walkthrough: MS looks like the illness, but it is the standard abbreviation for manuscript.
explanation.definitionFit: The two-letter form is the usual shortening of the word for a handwritten or typed document.

clue.text: Last guard for castle building

blocks.note: as food will last or stay fresh
the central tower of a fortress

explanation.surface: The final sentry posted for a fortress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guard' is a third meaning too: to keep something is to guard it.
explanation.definitionFit: Food keeps when it endures, and the strongest tower inside a fortress is its stronghold.
